vignette: Clinical Vignette: John's Story John, a 42-year-old electrician of Oceania descent, has been struggling with persistent symptoms following an assault that occurred late one evening while he was working alone. The event left him feeling vulnerable and exposed, deeply altering his sense of safety and self-worth. On the day of the incident, John had stayed late at work to finish a job. As dusk approached, an assailant suddenly broke in, causing John immense fear and trauma. Since then, the exact time of day when the assault occurred triggers intense distress for him. The moment the clock approaches that hour, he begins feeling detached and unreal, as if he is slipping into another dimension where danger lurks around every corner. These triggers have led John to engage in several maladaptive strategies to cope with his anxiety. He spends long hours on his phone, playing games or browsing the internet to distract himself from thinking about the assault. Drinking alcohol has also become a common way for him to numb his emotions and avoid the memories that haunt him. Over time, this reliance on substance use has deepened his sense of hopelessness and character blame. John's guilt is palpable whenever he recalls specific snapshots of the event-the assailant breaking in through the door, the sudden movement causing him to freeze with fear. Each memory feels like a separate picture, fragmented and incomplete, leaving him wondering what else he might be missing. The guilt intensifies as he questions why this happened to him, believing it's because of something inherently wrong within himself. The feeling that his character is flawed has led John to perceive the world as more dangerous than before. He reacts with alarm at unexpected movements or touches from others, and this heightened state of alertness often makes social interactions difficult. His wife notices how he startsleasily when she approaches him unexpectedly, which has strained their relationship. In addition to avoiding unfamiliar places due to his fear of not being able to assess the danger, John also avoids watching TV programs or reading about similar events because they trigger flashbacks and overwhelming guilt. The memory of the assault continues to play a significant role in his life; he feels like he is stuck reliving the moments over and over again. John's maladaptive strategies have further contributed to his negative appraisals. Spending long hours on his phone distracts him from addressing his underlying fears, but it also reinforces his belief that he has no future or worth as a person. The substance use exacerbates this sense of hopelessness, making it difficult for him to see any positive outcomes. The cycle of triggers leading to maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals has created a self-reinforcing loop that tightens over time. John's memory fragments are constantly triggered by the same time of day or auditory cues like doors slamming, which then lead to feelings of hopelessness and character blame. These negative thoughts further heighten his sense of threat and drive him back into maladaptive coping mechanisms. Despite his efforts to manage through avoidance and substance use, the cumulative impact on John's life has become overwhelming. His work as an electrician is increasingly difficult because he avoids going to unfamiliar places or working late hours when the assault occurred. His wife is concerned about how much time he spends alone, often isolating himself from family activities. What finally brought John to seek help was his growing realization that these strategies were no longer sufficient to manage his distress. He fears continuing down this path will lead him further into isolation and despair. Despite the overwhelming sense of hopelessness, John is also hopeful for a future where he can feel safe and in control again.
